(Nasdaq: SGP) (“SpyGlass Pharma”), a late-stage biopharmaceutical company, today announced the closing of its initial public offering of 10,781,250 shares of its common stock, which includes the exercise in full of the underwriters’ option to purchase 1,406,250 additional shares of its common stock, at a public offering price of $16.00 per share. The aggregate gross proceeds from the offering were $172.5 million, before deducting underwriting discounts and commissions and other offering expenses payable by SpyGlass Pharma. All shares of common stock were offered by SpyGlass Pharma. SpyGlass Pharma’s common stock began trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol “SGP” on February 6, 2026. Jefferies, Leerink Partners, Citigroup and Stifel acted as joint book-running managers for the offering. A registration statement relating to the offering has been filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission and became effective on January 30, 2026. The offering was made only by means of a prospectus. Copies of the final prospectus related to the offering are available at www.sec.gov. About SpyGlass Pharma SpyGlass Pharma is a late-stage biopharmaceutical company dedicated to transforming the treatment paradigm for patients living with chronic eye conditions through long-acting, sustained drug delivery of approved medicines. The company’s mission is to significantly improve the lives of patients with chronic eye conditions by developing durable drug delivery solutions that can empower patients and surgeons with confidence in long-term disease control and vision preservation. The SpyGlass Pharma platform, a novel, non-bioerodible drug delivery technology, is designed to be used with various well-established, approved medicines, including bimatoprost and other small molecules, providing flexibility to potentially treat a range of conditions in the front and back of the eye. The company was founded in 2019 by Malik Y. Kahook, M.D. and Glenn Sussman to solve the lack of ophthalmic innovations that capitalize on durable treatment options. The SpyGlass Pharma platform was originally developed in the Sue Anschutz-Rodgers Eye Center at the University of Colorado Anschutz School of Medicine. title: The 2026 AI Commerce Operating Plan for DTC CMOs
summary: A practical 2026 plan for channel diversification, catalog readiness, ownership, and measurement across AI shopping surfaces.
body_text: You do not need a separate growth strategy for every new shopping interface. You need one 2026 operating plan that protects current revenue, reduces dependence on any single acquisition channel, and makes the catalog usable wherever customers research products. AI shopping belongs inside that plan. ChatGPT supports product discovery from merchant catalog data, while search engines, marketplaces, retailer apps, and brand sites continue to shape the same purchase. The CMO's job is to coordinate the work without pretending that a new surface already has mature attribution or predictable media economics. Set the 2026 objective The goal is not to replace paid search, paid social, email, retail, or organic search. It is to build another route to qualified discovery while improving the product data that all of those channels use. Write the objective in operating terms: Improve coverage of high-value buyer questions. Make priority product facts accurate and available across destinations. Increase the number of acquisition paths the team can observe and learn from. Connect referrals and orders where the available data supports attribution. Do not attach an arbitrary revenue forecast to the channel. Start with a baseline and earn the right to set a target. Diversify without starving proven channels Channel diversification is a portfolio decision. Review the marginal performance of current spending, then fund a defined body of work instead of choosing a universal percentage. Protect the base Keep the programs that produce qualified demand at an acceptable cost. AI shopping readiness is not a reason to cut branded search, lifecycle, retail, or high-performing prospecting without evidence. Fund shared infrastructure Some of the most useful work is not channel-specific: Cleaning product attributes and taxonomy Resolving differences in price, availability, variants, and claims Publishing buying guidance based on real customer questions Improving referral and order tagging Establishing a repeatable visibility review These changes can support the storefront, feeds, search, marketplaces, and shopping assistants together. The catalog enrichment workflow provides one model for organizing the catalog portion. Use a test budget with a written scope Define what the test pays for, who owns it, and when it will be reviewed. A useful first scope could cover one category, 20 priority SKUs, 10 buyer questions, two AI shopping surfaces, and one measurement cycle. Adjust the amount to your economics rather than copying a benchmark from another brand. Make product and catalog readiness a CMO concern Merchandising and catalog operations own product truth, but growth depends on that truth traveling correctly. The CMO should make the gaps visible and ensure they have owners. Start from buyer decisions Use support tickets, reviews, onsite search, sales conversations, and return reasons to identify the facts customers need. Depending on the category, that may include: Dimensions, materials, ingredients, or technical specifications Fit, compatibility, age range, or intended use Variant relationships and availability Care, warranty, return, and delivery information Claims that require review or substantiation Fix the source of truth Do not patch one product page while the feed, marketplace listing, and support documentation remain inconsistent. Decide where each fact lives and how it reaches every destination. Shopify's product taxonomy and category metafields are one official model for structured category data. Other commerce systems offer their own product and attribute structures. Add a weekly exception review The meeting should focus on exceptions, not a broad status update. Review missing fields, conflicting claims, stale availability, unexplained visibility changes, and work that is blocked across teams. A free catalog and visibility audit can establish the first backlog. Assign ownership across functions One leader should run the operating cadence, but the work should remain cross-functional. Growth owns the buyer-question set, channel portfolio, and weekly review. Merchandising approves product facts, comparisons, and category priorities. Catalog operations maintains fields, variants, and feed quality. Content and communications produce useful product education and accurate third-party briefs. Engineering and analytics support distribution, referral tracking, and checkout handoffs where relevant. A new job title is optional. Clear decision rights are not. For many teams, an existing growth or ecommerce leader can own the program if catalog and engineering counterparts have committed time. Measure observations before outcomes AI shopping measurement is uneven. Some surfaces expose referrals or sources. Others do not. Responses can change with wording, context, location, and product availability. Maintain a visibility observation set Choose a stable group of buyer questions and record the exact wording, date, surface, brand mention, product mention, cited source where shown, and factual errors. Call these observations, not universal rankings. Wildcard's prompt tracking page explains this review model. Track catalog readiness For priority SKUs, report the share of required attributes that are present, verified, and current. Separate missing fields from fields that exist but contain weak or conflicting values. Track attributable commerce carefully Use referral parameters, platform reports, checkout data, and order records when they are available. Keep direct attribution separate from modeled or self-reported influence. Do not force a return-on-ad-spend model onto unpaid discovery or claim that a catalog edit caused revenue from a single before-and-after observation. Keep business outcomes in view The eventual scorecard can include qualified referrals, assisted conversions, new-customer orders, and revenue tied to a defensible source. Until those signals are reliable, report what the team shipped and what changed in the observation set. Run the first 90 days Days 1 to 30: Baseline Pick one category. Define the buyer-question set, audit priority SKUs, document current referrals and orders, and name owners for the first fixes. Days 31 to 60: Ship Correct the most important facts at the source, distribute them to relevant destinations, publish any missing buying guidance, and confirm analytics tagging. Record release dates so later analysis has a trustworthy timeline. Days 61 to 90: Review Repeat the same observations. Check catalog changes for accuracy, compare channel data, and decide whether to expand, revise, or stop each test. Scale the operating loop only after the team can maintain the first category. What to do this week Choose one priority category and 10 buyer questions grounded in customer language. Audit 20 SKUs for the facts needed to answer those questions. Name one operating owner and one approver from merchandising. Record a baseline across two relevant AI shopping surfaces and current referral analytics. Fund three source-of-truth fixes with a review date instead of setting an arbitrary channel budget. title: Franklin Electric Reports Fourth Quarter 2025 and Full Year 2025 Results
summary: Franklin Electric Reports Fourth Quarter 2025 and Full Year 2025 Results
body_text: Fort Wayne, IN – February 17, 2026 – Franklin Electric Co., Inc. today announced its fourth quarter and full year financial results for fiscal year 2025. Fourth quarter 2025 net sales were $506.9 million compared to fourth quarter 2024 net sales of $485.7 million. Fourth quarter 2025 operating income was $51.6 million, compared to fourth quarter 2024 operating income of $43.0 million. Fourth quarter 2025 diluted EPS was $0.87, compared to fourth quarter 2024 EPS of $0.72. Full year 2025 net sales were $2.1 billion compared to full year 2024 net sales of $2.0 billion. Full year 2025 operating income was $269.0 million, compared to full year 2024 operating income of $243.6 million. Full year 2025 diluted EPS was $3.22, compared to full year 2024 EPS of $3.86. Full year 2025 adjusted diluted EPS was $4.14, up $0.22 or 6 percent, compared to full year 2024. “The fourth quarter marked a solid close to a strong year of growth, expanded margins, and strong overall execution. For the full year, results were supported by effective pricing actions, transformation initiatives, and continued progress on our strategic investments in innovation and targeted acquisitions. We also strengthened our operating capabilities with our efforts to expand and optimize our global manufacturing footprint, positioning Franklin Electric to better serve customers and support future growth,” commented Joe Ruzynski, Franklin Electric’s CEO. “While macroeconomic conditions remain dynamic, we enter the new year with healthy order trends and a solid balance sheet with the flexibility to fuel our balanced approach to capital allocation. As we look ahead, our focus remains on driving profitable growth, expanding margins, and executing our strategic priorities to deliver long-term value for our shareholders,” concluded Mr. Ruzynski. body_text: View All News MDU Resources Reports 2025 Year-End Results; Initiates 2026 Guidance February 5, 2026 Net income of $190.4 million and earnings per share of $0.93 Income from continuing operations of $191.4 million, up $10.3 million year-over-year Utility rate base grew 16.0% year-over-year including the 49% ownership stake in Badger Wind Farm 2026 guidance: earnings per share in the range of $0.93 to $1.00 BISMARCK, N.D. , Feb. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- MDU Resources Group, Inc. (NYSE: MDU) today announced its financial results for 2025, reflecting continued execution of the company's strategy as a pure-play regulated energy delivery business. During 2025, the company advanced significant infrastructure investments, achieved customer growth across its electric and natural gas utilities, and benefited from key pipeline expansion projects recently placed into service, despite higher operating costs and weather-related variability. "2025 was a transformative year for our company," said Nicole A. Kivisto, president and CEO of MDU Resources. "In our first full year operating as a pure-play business, I am extremely proud of the team's performance. We deployed $792 million of capital that advanced key projects, including the 49% ownership acquisition of Badger Wind Farm, we made meaningful progress on regulatory initiatives, particularly within our natural gas distribution segment, and we delivered strong results in our pipeline segment, driven by new projects and strong short-term firm capacity demand." The following summarizes the company's year-end results for the twelve months ended Dec. 31: 2025 2024 (In millions, except per share amounts) Net income $ 190.4 $ 281.1 Earnings per share, diluted $ 0.93 $ 1.37 Income from continuing operations $ 191.4 $ 181.1 Earnings per share from continuing operations, diluted $ 0.93 $ 0.88 On Oct. 31, 2024, MDU Resources successfully completed the spinoff of Everus, which became an independent, publicly-traded company. Prior period results have been restated to reflect the spinoff. Everus' historical results of operations and certain costs associated with the spinoff are reported as discontinued operations. "As we continue in 2026, we are focused on executing a disciplined capital plan of approximately $560 million, advancing key regulatory activity across our jurisdictions and progressing major pipeline projects," Kivisto added. "With earnings guidance of $0.93 to $1.00 per share and continued customer growth, along with our employees' commitment to operational excellence, we are well positioned to meet rising demand while delivering long-term value for stockholders, customers and the communities we serve." Electric Utility Segment Electric earnings declined due mainly to higher operation and maintenance expense Electric utility earnings down $9.9 million year-over-year, totaling $64.9 million Higher operation and maintenance expense Benefited from retail sales revenue and volumes, including contributions from data centers The electric utility segment's 2025 results were influenced by higher operation and maintenance expense, primarily due to increased payroll-related costs. Additional cost pressures included planned outage-related costs at Coyote generating station, increased software expenses and higher insurance expense. These impacts were partially offset by higher retail sales revenue and volumes, driven in part by a data center near Ellendale, North Dakota. The electric segment continued to invest in system reliability and generation resources, including the 49% ownership interest in Badger Wind Farm, which was acquired and placed in service on Dec. 31, 2025. Electric Utility Segment Regulatory Updates: Montana: Filed a general rate case on Sept. 30, 2025, requesting an annual revenue increase of $14.1 million. The Montana Public Service Commission (MTPSC) has nine months to rule on the case. The company requested interim rates be effective Jan. 1, 2026. The MTPSC denied the interim rate relief, and a request for reconsideration was filed Dec. 26, 2025. On Feb. 3, 2026, the request for reconsideration went before the MTPSC and no action was taken. Wyoming: Filed a general rate case on June 30, 2025, requesting an annual revenue increase of $7.5 million. On Jan. 23, 2026, a settlement agreement was filed with an annual increase of $5.8 million and a stipulation to withdraw the Reliability and Safety Rider. Rates are anticipated to be effective April 1, 2026. North Dakota: Filed an updated Renewable Resource Cost Adjustment (RRCA) on Oct. 31, 2025, including recovery of Badger Wind Farm, and the North Dakota Public Service Commission approved the RRCA on Jan. 26, 2026. South Dakota: Filed an out-of-period update to the Infrastructure Rider on Oct. 31, 2025, reflecting inclusion of recovery for Badger Wind Farm. Natural Gas Distribution Segment Natural gas distribution earnings increased due primarily to rate relief Natural gas distribution earnings up $9.2 million year-over-year, totaling $56.1 million Rate relief in Washington, Montana, South Dakota and Wyoming Total retail customers grew 1.6% year-over-year Increased earnings partially offset by higher operation and maintenance expense The natural gas distribution segment's 2025 results improved year-over-year, driven primarily by rate relief across multiple jurisdictions, including Washington, Montana, South Dakota and Wyoming. These favorable impacts were partially offset by higher operation and maintenance expense, mainly due to increased insurance expense, higher payroll-related costs and increased software expenses. Natural Gas Distribution Segment Regulatory Updates: Washington: Implemented the multi-year rate plan approved on Feb. 24, 2025, with a year one annual increase of $29.8 million, effective March 5, 2025. On June 1, 2025, a revision to rates was effective, reducing year one revenue by $3.7 million related to forecasted capital projects that were not placed in service. On March 1, 2026, year two rates reflecting a $10.8 million annual increase will go into effect, subject to completion of a provisional plant review. Oregon: Filed a general rate case on Nov. 25, 2025, requesting $16.4 million annually. Rates are anticipated to be effective Oct. 31, 2026. Idaho: A general rate case settlement agreement was approved Dec. 30, 2025, for an annual increase of $13.0 million, with rates effective Jan. 1, 2026. Montana: On Jan. 14, 2025, interim natural gas rates were approved at $7.7 million annually, effective Feb. 1, 2025. A general rate case settlement was approved Oct. 7, 2025, finalizing a $7.3 million annual increase, with rates effective Nov. 1, 2025. Wyoming: General rate case settlement agreement approved June 24, 2025, for an annual increase of $2.1 million, with rates effective Aug. 1, 2025. Pipeline Segment Expansion projects continue to drive earnings, largely offset by higher operation and maintenance expense as well as the absence of one-time benefits in 2024 Pipeline segment record earnings of $68.2 million, up slightly year-over-year Higher transportation revenue, mainly from expansion projects and increased demand for short-term firm capacity contracts Higher operation and maintenance expense The pipeline segment delivered strong performance in 2025. Earnings benefited from increased transportation revenue associated with expansion projects completed throughout 2024 and the Minot Expansion Project placed in service in November 2025. The company also benefited from increased customer demand for short-term firm capacity contracts. These favorable factors were largely offset by higher operation and maintenance expense, primarily due to increased payroll-related expenses, higher depreciation related to increased capital investments, and higher property taxes, particularly in Montana, as well as the absence of 2024 benefits, including the proceeds from a customer settlement and an adjustment related to effective state income tax rate change. Pipeline Segment Strategic Projects Updates: Minot Expansion Project: The expansion was placed in service Nov. 1, 2025, and adds approximately seven million cubic feet per day of natural gas transportation capacity. Line Section 32 Expansion Project: This project will provide natural gas transportation service to a new electric generation facility in northwest North Dakota. The company continues to make progress on required surveys and anticipates filing its FERC application in March of 2026. Construction is targeted to be complete in late 2028. Minot Industrial Project: This proposed project could consist of an approximately 90-mile pipeline from Tioga, North Dakota to Minot, North Dakota and ancillary facilities to support anticipated industrial demand in the area. The company has signed an agreement to support the early-stage development of the project through the second quarter of 2026. Bakken East Project: The FERC pre-filing request was submitted Dec. 23, 2025 for the proposed pipeline project from the Bakken region in western North Dakota to eastern North Dakota. A binding open season launched Feb. 2, 2026, and will close March 13, 2026. The company continues contract negotiations with several interested parties. Guidance For 2026, MDU Resources expects earnings per share to be in the range of $0.93 to $1.00. In addition, the company has $560 million in capital investment planned for 2026. The expected 2026 results are based on these assumptions: Normal weather, economic and operating conditions Continued growth in utility customers at 1%–2% annually Successful execution of approved capital investment and rate recovery plans The company's long-term EPS guidance remains unchanged with an expected growth rate of 6%–8%. Equity and Funding Plan On Dec. 5, 2025, the company completed a follow-on public offering of 10,152,284 shares of its common stock at a public offering price of $19.70 per share. In addition, on Dec. 23, 2025, the underwriters exercised their option to purchase 1,522,842 additional shares of common stock. Pursuant to forward sale agreements entered into in connection with the offering, the company has discretion to settle the forward sale agreements on one or more settlement dates prior to Dec. 6, 2027, subject to certain price adjustments as set forth in the forward sale agreements as well as transaction and other associated fees. The company had previously stated that it expects to issue between $150 million to $175 million of equity in 2026, and between $100 million to $125 million in 2027, to support near-term capital expenditures for growth. The 11,675,126 shares of common stock in the forward sale agreements is expected to meet a substantial portion of these stated equity issuance needs. The company will assess equity issuance needs beyond 2027 in future periods as its long-term investment plans are updated. Corporate Strategy MDU Resources is committed to its CORE strategy, which prioritizes customers and communities, operational excellence, returns focused initiatives and an employee-driven culture. The company anticipates a capital investment of approximately $3.1 billion for 2026-2030 and customer growth of 1%–2% annually. Additionally, the company anticipates 6%–8% long-term compound annual growth on earnings per share while targeting a 60%–70% annual dividend payout ratio. Select "Events & Presentations," and click on "Year-End 2025 Earnings Conference Call." A replay of the webcast will be available at the same location. About MDU Resources Group, Inc. MDU Resources Group, Inc., a member of the S&P SmallCap 600 index, strives to deliver safe, reliable, cost-effective and environmentally responsible electric utility and natural gas distribution services to more than 1.2 million customers across the Pacific Northwest and Midwest. In addition to its utility operations, the company's pipeline business operates a more than 3,800-mile natural gas pipeline network and storage system, ensuring reliable energy delivery across the Northern Plains. Your Longevity Baseline: 12 Health Markers Worth Knowing And Tracking
summary: Learn how to build a longevity baseline with daily-life signals and medical benchmarks, so you can spot change early and support healthspan over time.
body_text: Health has moved to the forefront of how people think about daily life. In that renewed focus, longevity has become a practical extension, shifting attention from simply adding years to protecting what those years feel like. As a society, we’ve made real progress on lifespan. Modern medicine helps more people survive serious diagnoses and emergencies than ever before. The bigger challenge now is what happens next: protecting your strength, mobility, metabolism, and brain health for decades. The tradeoff is that many of the biggest threats to your quality of life now move slowly. Symptoms like high blood pressure, blood sugar drift, plaque buildup, sleep debt, loss of strength, and chronic inflammation often build for years before they announce themselves. This is why longevity matters, and why it can’t be treated like a wellness trend. Longevity isn’t about chasing a perfect routine. It’s about understanding what your body’s doing under the surface and noticing early shifts in key markers while you still have simple, realistic options. Longevity starts with knowing a core set of benchmarks that tend to predict how well you age. Some are facts you can learn once and keep on file. Some are signals you’ll notice in your daily life. Others come from lab work and age-appropriate screening. Together, these markers create a clearer picture of your baseline, and they help you recognize when something is changing. Your Longevity Baseline Your longevity baseline is your personal record of the health markers that most directly shape how well you’ll age. It’s most likely not a single app or document, and it’s not something your doctor “keeps for you.” It’s the information you collect and keep accessible so you can understand what’s normal for your body, recognize gradual change early, and help establish a clearer context when making healthcare decisions. Most people will never track sleep, steps, labs, screenings, and blood pressure in a single place, and they don’t need to. The goal isn’t consolidation. The goal is clarity. You want to know which markers matter, where each one is captured, and how to find the numbers and dates when you need them. What information should be in your longevity baseline A practical longevity baseline includes two categories of markers. Daily life markers are signals you may notice or can measure outside of an appointment. They help you understand recovery, stress load, cardiovascular fitness, and trend changes that often show up before formal labs shift. Medical benchmarks are markers that come from routine healthcare, lab work, and preventive screening. They help quantify cardiometabolic risk, support early detection, and confirm whether symptoms have an underlying cause. When you track both categories, you get a more accurate picture of your health status. Daily life markers show how your body is functioning day-to-day and week-to-week. Medical benchmarks clarify what’s happening under the surface. Common tools for tracking your longevity baseline Most people don‘t track every health marker in one place, and they don’t need to. A longevity baseline works when you use the right tool for the right type of data, and know where to look for the data. Tools that capture daily life signals Wearables and phone health apps are best for tacking passive, repeatable data. They capture what your real data looks like without extra effort, which makes them useful for trends over time. Common signals include: Sleep duration and regularity Steps, movement minutes, and activity consistency Resting heart rate trends Weight Blood pressure Tools for medical benchmarks Lab results and screening reports typically live in your doctor’s patient portal. What makes them part of your longevity baseline is that you keep a quick-access summary, so you can see trends without digging through records or trying to remember passwords to multiple patient portals. That summary usually includes: Date and result for A1C or fasting glucose Date and result for lipid panel, including triglycerides Blood pressure trend, if measured in clinic Screening dates and outcomes based on age and risk Key family history and age of onset for major conditions For most people, this is one simple “baseline note” that captures highlights, even though the official documents live elsewhere. For others, they save and collect their summaries in a single digital or physical file. A practical approach to tracking your health You don’t need to move data from one tool to another. You need a system that’s easy to maintain and simple to reference, so you can answer two questions with confidence: what normal looks like for you, and what’s been changing long enough to deserve attention. With your longevity baseline in place, the next step is deciding what belongs on it. Not every health marker deserves the same amount of attention, and you don’t need to track everything. The goal is to focus on a short set of benchmarks that are both meaningful and practical, markers that connect directly to long-term function and can be checked often enough to show a trend. The benchmarks that follow are organized by ease. The first ones are facts you can confirm once and keep on file. Next are daily life signals that help you understand how your body’s functioning. The later benchmarks require lab work or screening. They can reveal risk long before symptoms force a medical decision. Each section explains more about what the data is, why the marker matters for longevity, what a healthy trend generally looks like, and how to use the information in real life. Marker 1: Your Blood Type Your blood type is the name for a very specific biological detail: what’s on the surface of your red blood cells. Red blood cells are your oxygen delivery system. On the outside of those cells are tiny molecular “tags” called antigens. Your immune system is basically a high-level security team, and it pays close attention to those tags. If unfamiliar tags show up in your bloodstream, your immune system may treat them like an intruder. This is why blood type matters so much in transfusions. Blood type is built from two labels. The first is the ABO system, which tells you whether your red blood cells carry the A tag, the B tag, both, or neither: If you have the A tag, your type is A If you have the B tag, your type is B If you have both A and B tags, your type is AB If you have neither A nor B tags, your type is O The second label is the Rh factor, which usually refers to one specific antigen called RhD: If you have the RhD tag, you’re positive If you don’t, you’re negative Combine those labels and you get the eight blood types you see in real life: A+, A-, B+, B-, AB+, AB-, O+, O-. Why your blood type matters for longevity Blood type matters most when timing matters. If you ever need blood products urgently, compatibility helps prevent dangerous transfusion reactions. In true emergencies, clinicians may use O- red blood cells when there isn’t time to confirm type because it’s broadly compatible for red cells. When plasma is needed quickly, AB plasma is often considered broadly compatible. Knowing your blood type ahead of time removes friction in a high-stakes moment. Blood type also shows up in research beyond transfusions. Some studies suggest associations between ABO blood type and certain health risks. For example, type O has been linked with a higher likelihood of stomach ulcers in some populations, while non-O blood types have been associated with a higher risk of clotting-related events. Some research has also suggested that certain non-O blood types may be linked with a higher risk of pancreatic cancer, while other findings have even explored potential links between AB blood type and cognitive outcomes. These associations don’t outweigh the biggest drivers of healthspan like blood pressure, blood sugar, lipids, sleep, activity, and strength. They’re simply part of the broader context of how bodies differ. How to find your blood type Finding your blood type is usually simple, but it may not be listed on routine lab work unless there was a reason to test it. Here are the most common ways people locate this information: Check your past medical records if you’ve had surgery, pregnancy care, transfusions, or certain hospital visits If you’ve ever donated blood or plasma, check your donation records or donor card If you can’t find it, you may simply need to ask your primary care clinician to order ABO and Rh typing Where keep track of your blood type Document your blood type and keep it where you can access quickly: Your phone’s Medical ID (along with allergies and medications) Your longevity baseline notes, where you keep key dates and results A wallet card, if you prefer a physical backup for emergencies Marker 2: Your Health History Your health history is the story your body’s already lived. It’s the running record of diagnoses you’ve had, surgeries or procedures you’ve been through, medications you take, allergies you react to, and anything that’s shaped how your body tends to respond under stress. It sounds basic, but it’s one of the most powerful longevity markers because it changes how clinicians assess risk, interpret symptoms, and choose the safest next step. Here’s the key idea: your health history isn’t just a list. It’s context. It tells your care team what your baseline looks like, what you’ve already tried, what you’ve tolerated well, and what you absolutely shouldn’t be given again. Why your health history matters for longevity A clear, accurate health history does three big things for healthspan. First, it reduces preventable errors. Medications, allergies, past reactions, and past procedures matter most when care is moving fast. If you’re sick, stressed, or in pain, memory gets unreliable. A clean record keeps important details from getting lost. Second, it speeds up better decisions. When a clinician knows your background, they can connect dots faster and avoid going down dead ends. That can mean fewer delays, fewer duplicate tests, and more precise recommendations. Finally, knowing your health history may help you spot patterns over time. Longevity is built on course-correcting early. If you can see that your blood pressure crept up after a certain medication change, or that your sleep was impacted after a work shift change, you’ve got something actionable instead of a vague feeling that you’re “off.” What to include in your health history At a minimum, your health history should include: Current diagnoses or ongoing conditions Surgeries, hospitalizations, and major injuries Medications you take now, including dose and how often you take them Supplements you take regularly Allergies and what reaction you had Past medications that didn’t work for you or caused side effects Any implanted devices or ongoing therapies you rely on Dates, even rough ones, for major events The name of the clinic or hospital, if you remember it Any patterns you’ve noticed, like symptoms that flare with stress or poor sleep How to find your health history Most people already have this information scattered across a few places. You’re just pulling it together. Start with: Your patient portals for your primary care clinician, specialists, or urgent care visits Your pharmacy history for an accurate medication list Any discharge paperwork you still have from surgeries, hospital visits, or imaging Your insurance explanation of benefits, which can jog your memory on dates and procedures Write what you know, document what you’re unsure about, and update it as you confirm details. Where to keep track of your health history Keep it in a place you can access quickly and update without effort: Your phone’s Medical ID for the essentials, especially allergies and medications Your longevity baseline notes as a longer version you can maintain over time A printed copy in a wallet, purse, or car if you want a physical backup If you only do one thing today, make sure your Medical ID has your current medications and allergies. This small step pays off immediately when it matters. Marker 3: Your Family Health History Your family health history is the health pattern you inherited, or at least the pattern you’re more likely to run into. It’s not fate, and it’s not a diagnosis. It’s a risk map. When clinicians know what runs in your family and when it showed up, they can make smarter decisions about screening, prevention, and how aggressively to manage certain markers. Most chronic diseases don’t arrive out of nowhere. They build over time. Family history helps you see where your personal “watch list” might need to be stronger, even if you feel great right now. Why your family health history matters for longevity Family history matters because it may change your probability landscape. If certain conditions show repeatedly in close relatives, especially at younger ages, your clinician may recommend earlier screening, more frequent monitoring, or a lower threshold for follow-up when symptoms appear. Familiarity with your family's health history also helps you interpret your own trends. The same blood pressure reading can carry a different level of concern depending on whether early heart disease, stroke, diabetes, or kidney disease is common in your family. This isn’t about alarm. It’s about precision. Longevity isn’t only about doing the basics. It’s about doing the basics with the right level of urgency for you. What should be included when tracking or documenting your family’s medical history You don’t need to build a family tree that belongs in a museum. You’re looking for patterns in first-degree relatives first, then second-degree relatives if you can. Start with parents, siblings, and children. Then add grandparents, aunts, uncles, and first cousins. The most useful details to capture are the condition, the age symptoms began or the age at diagnosis, and for any relatives who have died, their age at death and the cause, if you know it. You’ll capture a lot of longevity value by focusing on conditions that commonly affect healthspan and have clear screening or prevention pathways: Heart disease, heart attacks, and high blood pressure Stroke or blood clotting events Type 2 diabetes and metabolic disease High cholesterol Cancer patterns, especially colon, breast, ovarian, prostate, melanoma, and pancreatic Dementia or significant cognitive decline Osteoporosis and fragility fractures Autoimmune disease, if it’s clustered in close relatives Also note any “early” events. A heart attack or stroke at a younger age tends to change how clinicians approach risk. How to research or discover your family health history This is one of the only health markers you can’t get from a lab or wearable. You’ll need to gather this information from conversations with family members, or old medical records, if they’re willing to share. Ask relatives simple, direct questions: What conditions have you been treated for long term? Have you ever had a heart attack, stroke, or blood clot? Have you been diagnosed with diabetes or prediabetes? Has anyone in our family had cancer? What kind, and how old were they? Has anyone had dementia or major cognitive decline? Even partial answers or details from only a few relatives can be useful. The goal is to document possible risks and look for patterns that may shape your health over time. This information helps your medical team assess risk more accurately, and it can guide how you approach prevention, including what you prioritize and how early you start. Where to keep track of your family history Keep your family history in your longevity baseline notes so it’s easy to update as you learn more. If your clinician’s office has a patient intake form or a portal section for family history, fill it out, but don’t rely on that alone. Portals can have technical issues, doctors change, and details get lost. Having your own record also makes it much easier to complete intake forms when you’re seeing a new provider. Over time, family history becomes one of the most useful parts of your longevity baseline because it adds context to everything else you track. Marker 4: Your Blood Pressure Blood pressure is the force of blood pushing against the walls of your arteries every time your heart beats, and every moment between beats. Think of your arteries like a flexible hose system. Pressure that runs too high for too long doesn’t usually hurt in the moment, but it steadily stresses the lining of the vessels and the organs those vessels feed. That’s why blood pressure is one of the most important longevity markers: it affects your heart, brain, kidneys, and eyes over decades. Why your blood pressure matters for longevity High blood pressure is often called the silent risk for a reason. Many people feel completely fine while damage is quietly accumulating. Over time, elevated pressure accelerates atherosclerosis, increases strain on the heart, and raises the risk of stroke and kidney disease. It’s also strongly tied to brain health because your brain depends on small, delicate vessels that don’t tolerate chronic high pressure well. From a longevity standpoint, blood pressure is valuable because it’s measurable, modifiable, and predictive. It’s one of the clearest places where small changes now can protect the quality of life later. How to take your blood pressure You’ll usually see blood pressure measured in three places: At routine healthcare visits At many pharmacies or retail clinics with automated cuffs At home with a validated upper-arm cuff Home readings can be especially helpful because some people run higher in clinical settings due to stress, and others run higher in daily life but look fine in a quick office snapshot. If you’re going to track blood pressure at home, do it in a way that makes the number meaningful: Sit quietly for five minutes before measuring Keep both feet on the floor, back supported, arm supported at heart level Take two readings one minute apart Track the average, not the single best number How to interpret a blood pressure reading Blood pressure is written as systolic/diastolic , like 118/76 . It’s not a ratio. It’s two separate pressures measured at the same time. The top number is the systolic reading . It’s the peak pressure in your arteries at the moment your heart contracts and pushes blood forward. Think of it as the “push” phase. Systolic pressure is influenced by how strongly the heart is pumping, how stiff or flexible your arteries are, and how much resistance the blood is pushing against. The bottom number is diastolic . It’s the pressure that remains in your arteries between beats, when your heart relaxes and refills with blood. Think of it as the “resting” pressure in the system. Diastolic pressure reflects the baseline tension in your blood vessels and how easily blood can flow through them when the heart isn’t actively squeezing. Clinically, both numbers matter. Many people focus on the top number because it tends to rise with age as arteries stiffen, and it’s strongly tied to cardiovascular and stroke risk. The bottom number still matters because it reflects the pressure your vessels are under all the time, and it can be important in younger adults and in certain medical contexts. The key is that either number can be high, and either can drive risk. Clinicians don’t read those two numbers as a single combined score. They evaluate each number on its own , then classify the reading based on whichever number falls into the higher risk range. Normal blood pressure requires both numbers to be in range. If either number is elevated, the reading is treated as elevated. In U.S. clinical care, the most widely used categories come from the ACC/AHA guideline , and they break down like this for adults: Normal: systolic under 120 and diastolic under 80 Elevated: systolic 120 to 129 and diastolic under 80 High blood pressure, stage 1: systolic 130 to 139 or diastolic 80 to 89 High blood pressure, stage 2: systolic 140 or higher or diastolic 90 or higher A quick way to apply this: look at both numbers and let the higher category win. For example, 128/92 is considered high blood pressure because the diastolic number falls in the stage 2 range, even though the systolic number does not. Where to keep track of blood pressure Blood pressure is one of the few markers that can live in multiple places and still be useful: If you use a home cuff that stores readings, let it store them Keep your averaged results in your longevity baseline notes with dates If your patient portal stores clinic readings, use it as a reference, not your only record What to do with your blood pressure marker If your numbers are consistently elevated, it’s worth addressing sooner rather than later because early action is often simpler, more effective, and may protect long-term health. Start by confirming the trend with repeat readings, then bring those averages into a conversation with your clinician. If you’re already being treated, trends help you and your care team see whether your treatment plan is working. Marker 5: Your Cholesterol And Lipid Profile Cholesterol is a waxy, fat-like substance your body uses as raw material. It’s one of the building blocks that helps your cells hold their structure, and it’s involved in making certain hormones. Your liver also uses cholesterol to make bile, which helps you break down and absorb fats from food. Cholesterol and other fats don’t dissolve in blood the way sugar does. Your body has to move them around using tiny transport “packages.” These packages carry this fat from place to place, delivering what your body needs, and returning what your body doesn’t. When there’s more cholesterol riding around than your body can safely manage, the excess can start to deposit in places it doesn’t belong, including along your artery walls. Over time, those deposits can contribute to plaque buildup, which can narrow blood flow and raise cardiovascular risk. Cholesterol is often referred to as a single number, but clinically it’s actually a panel of markers that tell the story of how fats are being carried through your bloodstream. Why your cholesterol markers matter for longevity Cholesterol is essential. What matters is how much cholesterol is circulating, how it’s being carried, and whether that pattern increases the likelihood of plaque buildup over time. From a longevity standpoint, cholesterol markers matter because vascular disease is one of the most common threats to long-term function. When blood flow is compromised, your heart has to work harder, your brain becomes more vulnerable, and your ability to exercise, recover, and stay resilient declines. Cholesterol gives you an early window into cardiovascular risk, often years before symptoms show up. It’s one of the few markers that can flag a slow-building problem while you still have time to change the trajectory. Cholesterol also becomes more powerful when you interpret it alongside other markers. Elevated cholesterol plus elevated blood pressure is a different risk picture than elevated cholesterol alone. The same is true when blood sugar and triglycerides are trending up. This is why to include your lipid panel in your longevity baseline. How to get your cholesterol numbers and what they mean You typically check cholesterol with a lipid panel, a standard blood test your primary care clinician can order, and that’s often included in routine annual labs in adulthood. Depending on your risk factors and what your clinician is looking for, you may be asked to fast beforehand, especially when triglycerides are a key focus. Once the results are in, they’re usually easy to find in your patient portal under lab history. Most labs will show reference ranges, but the targets that matter most depend on your overall risk profile and health history. In general, trends usually matter more than a single result. The goal is to keep key numbers, especially LDL and triglycerides, from creeping upward over time. A standard lipid panel includes: LDL cholesterol, which reflects the cholesterol being carried in particles that tend to deliver it out into the body, including into artery walls. In general, lower LDL is associated with a lower risk of plaque buildup in arteries and supports lower long-term cardiovascular risk. HDL cholesterol, which reflects the cholesterol being carried in particles that help move it away from the bloodstream for processing. In general, higher HDL is often considered more protective. Triglycerides are circulating fats that reflect how your body is processing and storing energy. They often climb with excess refined carbohydrates, alcohol, weight gain, and reduced insulin sensitivity. When triglycerides run high and HDL runs low, it can be a sign your metabolism is under strain and your cardiovascular risk profile may be shifting. Total cholesterol adds up the cholesterol measured across different carriers. It’s a broad snapshot, but it can be misleading on its own because it doesn’t tell you how much is coming from LDL versus HDL. The component numbers are what guide risk assessment. The simple takeaway is this: a lipid panel shows how fats are being transported in your body. If you’ve been told your numbers are “borderline,” don’t ignore this advice. Borderline is often the stage where course correction is simplest and most effective. Where to keep track of your cholesterol numbers For longevity tracking, you don’t need every line item from every test. You need the headline numbers and the dates. Keep a quick-access summary in your longevity baseline notes: Date of test LDL HDL Triglycerides Total cholesterol or non-HDL, if listed What to do with the information about your cholesterol trends If your LDL, triglycerides, or overall lipid pattern is trending in the wrong direction, start by looking at the inputs that most reliably move the numbers. Sleep quality affects metabolic regulation. Consistent movement helps your body use fats and sugars more efficiently. Fiber-forward eating patterns can support healthier lipid balance over time. Alcohol can push triglycerides up in a way that’s easy to miss. Weight changes can matter too, but only if weight is a meaningful clinical marker for you. The goal is identifying the most realistic lever you can pull consistently, then rechecking your labs so you can see whether the trend shifted. From there, get specific with your clinician based on your full risk picture. Cholesterol targets aren’t one-size-fits-all. Family history, blood pressure, blood sugar, age, and prior cardiovascular events all change what “acceptable” means and how aggressively you should manage a rising LDL or triglyceride pattern. If you’re already on a cholesterol-lowering medication, your lipid panel becomes your progress check. It shows whether your treatment plan is working and gives you and your clinician a clear path forward for better protecting long-term cardiovascular health. Marker 6: Your Resting Heart Rate Resting heart rate is the number of times your heart beats per minute when your body is calm and still. It’s a simple measurement with deep physiology behind it, because it reflects how your heart, blood vessels, nervous system, and metabolism are working together in the background. Your heart’s job is to deliver oxygen-rich blood to tissues. To do that, it relies on two levers: how much blood it pumps per beat (stroke volume) and how often it beats (heart rate). When stroke volume is strong and your cardiovascular system runs efficiently, your heart can meet baseline demand with fewer beats. When your body is under higher internal load, your nervous system often increases heart rate to maintain output. Internal load can come from many places, including poor sleep, dehydration, low aerobic conditioning, illness, heat, stimulants, alcohol, stress, or a training schedule outpacing recovery. Resting heart rate becomes more meaningful once you separate “today’s number” from your baseline. Most people carry a personal range. Your goal is to learn your usual range during normal life, then use changes as a signal. Why resting heart rate matters for longevity Resting heart rate matters because it acts like a proxy for cardiovascular efficiency plus recovery capacity. Over time, higher resting heart rate has been associated with higher cardiovascular risk and all-cause mortality, while lower resting heart rate often reflects better aerobic conditioning and lower sympathetic nervous system drive. The point isn’t chasing an ideal number. The value comes from understanding your baseline and protecting it. From a longevity lens, resting heart rate earns a place on your baseline for two reasons. First, it can change long before you feel “unhealthy.” Second, it responds to modifiable inputs. When resting heart rate runs persistently higher than your normal range, it often signals a mismatch between demand and recovery. Catching that early supports course correction while options remain straightforward. How to measure resting heart rate Resting heart rate is most useful when the measurement conditions stay consistent. A practical approach looks like this: Wearable or phone health app : Useful for long-term trends. Single readings vary, but multi-day averages often track well. Manual check : In the morning, before caffeine and before activity, sit quietly for five minutes. Take your pulse for thirty seconds and multiply by two. Clinic readings : Helpful context, but clinic conditions vary. Use them as a reference point, not your only data source. I f you want one “clean” baseline method, use the morning seated measurement for several days, then use the average as your anchor. What your resting heart rate generally means Many healthy adults fall somewhere between 60 and 100 beats per minute at rest, with plenty of normal variation. Regular endurance training often produces resting heart rates below 60, sometimes much lower. Higher numbers can still be normal in certain contexts, including anxiety, dehydration, fever, poor sleep, nicotine use, stimulant use, anemia, thyroid dysfunction, or low aerobic conditioning. What matters most clinically is context plus persistence. A single high day rarely carries meaning on its own. A sustained upward shift from your usual baseline carries more signal, especially when paired with fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance, or palpitations. How target heart rate fits in this discussion While your resting heart rate tells you your cardiovascular system baseline. Your target heart rate tells you whether your workout intensity sits in a range that supports cardiovascular conditioning. The American Heart Association’s target heart rate chart uses an age-based estimate for maximum heart rate (often approximated as 220 minus your age ), then defines moderate intensity as about 50 to 70 percent of that maximum and vigorous intensity as about 70 to 85 percent . Where to keep track of resting heart rate You don’t need a complex system. You need consistency. If you use a wearable, let it capture and store daily data, then use it to monitor your usual range over time. In your longevity baseline notes, add a simple monthly check-in with your typical resting heart rate range plus any clear reason for a change, like travel, illness, or a major routine shift. This keeps the record usable without turning it into homework. What to do with a sustained resting heart rate increase If resting heart rate rises above your baseline and remains elevated for more than a week or two, treat it as clinically useful information. Start with the inputs most likely to influence it: sleep consistency, hydration status, alcohol intake, stress load, stimulant use, and training volume. If routine remains stable and resting heart rate remains higher than baseline, bring the pattern into a conversation with your clinician, especially alongside unusual shortness of breath, chest discomfort, dizziness, fainting, or persistent palpitations. Resting heart rate is a simple marker with high clinical value. It reflects cardiovascular efficiency and recovery, and it can signal reduced resilience early, before more obvious symptoms surface. Marker 7: Your Sleep Duration And Regularity Sleep looks passive from the outside, but physiologically it’s one of your most active repair states. During sleep, your nervous system shifts gears, stress hormones recalibrate, tissues recover, and the brain runs critical maintenance programs tied to memory, mood, and metabolic control. For longevity tracking, sleep works best as two markers, not one. Duration answers how much sleep you get across a typical week. Regularity answers how consistent your sleep timing stays from night to night. Both matter. A person can hit a solid weekly average and still run on a circadian schedule that keeps their body in a constant state of catch-up. Why sleep matters for longevity Sleep influences many of the same systems you’re tracking through blood pressure, lipids, and glucose. Short or irregular sleep can increase sympathetic nervous system tone, limit the normal overnight “dip” in blood pressure, and raise stress hormone output. It can also worsen insulin sensitivity, shift appetite regulation, and amplify inflammation, all of which can nudge cardiometabolic risk in the wrong direction over time. Sleep also protects brain health . Consolidation of learning and memory depends on healthy sleep architecture, including predictable cycling through non-REM and REM stages. Nights with fragmented sleep often deliver less restorative value, even when total time in bed looks fine. From a healthspan lens, sleep earns a spot on your longevity baseline because it’s both predictive and modifiable. Better sleep supports recovery, training adaptation, emotional regulation, and cognitive resilience. Poor sleep quietly erodes those foundations. How to measure sleep duration and regularity Sleep tracking doesn't require perfection. It requires consistency. Most people measure sleep using one of three approaches: Wearable or phone health app: Best for passive trends across weeks and months. Single-night staging can be noisy, but weekly averages often stay useful. Simple sleep log: Bedtime, wake time, night awakenings, plus a one-line note on alcohol, travel, illness, or stress spikes. Hybrid approach: Wearable for trends, notes for context. The most useful sleep numbers tend to be: Average sleep duration across seven days Bedtime and wake time consistency Time awake during the night, especially when it increases over multiple weeks What healthy sleep baseline generally looks like Most adults function best with a stable sleep window plus enough total sleep to support daytime energy, mood, training recovery, and cognitive sharpness. For many people, seven to nine hours becomes a workable target range, but the more important signal is how you feel plus how stable your pattern stays. Regularity often shows up as a quieter nervous system. Energy feels steadier. Cravings feel less extreme. Workouts recover better. Mood swings soften. Those changes can show up before labs move. Where to keep track of sleep Let a wearable or phone app store the nightly data. In your longevity baseline notes, keep a simple monthly summary: average sleep duration, a rough description of schedule consistency, plus any major disruptor such as travel, illness, shift changes, or a high-stress period. You’ll end up with trend visibility without turning sleep into a full-time project. Marker 8: Your Weekly Movement Minutes And Activity Consistency Movement is one of the few longevity inputs that touches almost every system you care about: cardiovascular function, metabolism, muscle, joint resilience, and brain health. Clinically, it helps to think in two categories. Aerobic activity improves cardiovascular conditioning and how efficiently your body uses oxygen. Strength work uses resistance to preserve muscle, support bone density, and reinforce balance and mobility for daily life. Once you understand those two categories, the next variable is intensity. The body adapts to the demand you place on it, so the benefit you get from activity depends on pace, not only duration. A practical way to gauge intensity without equipment is the talk test. During moderate activity, you can speak in short sentences. During vigorous activity, speech usually drops to a few words before you need a breath. Why movement matters for longevity From a longevity standpoint, the most important feature of movement is repeatability. Aerobic activity supports vascular function, blood pressure regulation, insulin sensitivity, lipid metabolism, and brain blood flow. Strength work protects muscle mass, connective tissue capacity, and the physical reserve that keeps you independent. Those benefits build when activity is consistent, because your body adapts to repeated exposure. A steady weekly pattern supports recovery, maintains function, and helps preserve independence over time. How to track movement minutes and consistency You’re tracking activity for one reason: to make the goal measurable, then see whether your week-to-week pattern supports the level of conditioning you want. Guidelines give you a clinically grounded target range, then your own tracking shows how close your real life gets. The American Heart Association generally recommend at least 150 minutes per week of moderate-intensity aerobic activity or 75 minutes per week of vigorous activity, plus muscle-strengthening activity on two or more days per week . The World Health Organization keeps the same minimum target, then extends the range for additional benefit: 150 to 300 minutes per week of moderate-intensity aerobic activity (or the vigorous equivalent) for many adults. For tracking, simplicity wins. A wearable or phone health app can capture minutes, steps, and active time passively. If you don’t use wearables, a weekly log or workout journal works well. Track total aerobic minutes plus the number of strength sessions. Add one brief note when context changes, such as travel, illness, heat, injury flare, or a major schedule shift. Where to keep track of your movement baseline Let a wearable or phone app store daily data. In your longevity baseline notes, keep a monthly snapshot: typical weekly aerobic minutes, typical strength sessions per week, and any clear reason for a sustained change. This creates a usable trend record without turning movement into admin work. What to do with the information If weekly minutes dip for a couple weeks, treat it as a planning problem, not a motivation problem. Look for the smallest repeatable dose you can protect on busy days, then build upward. If weekly minutes rise but recovery worsens, adjust intensity, sleep consistency, hydration, or strength volume before adding more. The goal is a sustainable pattern, because long-term adaptation follows long-term repetition. Marker 9: Your Waist Size And Waist-To-Height Ratio Waist size is a simple measurement with a surprisingly deep clinical story. It estimates how much tissue sits around your midsection, including visceral fat; the type stored deeper in the abdomen around your organs. Visceral fat behaves differently than the fat stored under the skin. It’s metabolically active, meaning it can influence inflammation, insulin sensitivity, triglycerides, and blood pressure over time. Two people can weigh the same and have very different risk profiles depending on where tissue is stored, which is why clinicians often pay attention to waist size as part of a longevity baseline. Waist size also has a practical advantage. Unlike many lab markers, you can measure it at home with a tape measure, track it over time, and use the trend in early context alongside blood pressure, lipids, and blood sugar. Why waist size matters for longevity From a healthspan lens, waist size is less about appearance and more about cardiometabolic risk. A rising waist trend can signal rising visceral fat, which often travels with higher triglycerides, lower HDL, higher blood pressure, and reduced insulin sensitivity. Those shifts raise the likelihood of atherosclerosis and vascular disease over time, which can affect stamina, recovery, brain resilience, and long-term independence. Waist size also helps with timing. When your waist trend starts moving up, many people still feel fine. Catching the shift early keeps options broader and usually keeps the plan simpler. How to measure waist size For tracking, the most important rule is consistency. Pick one measurement method and stick with it. A clean home method: Stand tall, feet hip-width apart, relaxed abdomen, normal posture Wrap a tape measure around your waist at the level of your hip bones, keeping the tape horizontal Keep the tape measure snug, not compressing skin Measure at the end of a normal exhale Take two readings and record the average If you’d rather use the belly button as a landmark, that can work too. Just stay consistent with the same landmark each time so the trend stays meaningful. How to interpret waist size Waist size is a screening marker, not a diagnosis. Clinicians pay attention to it because a larger waist often reflects more abdominal fat, including visceral fat, the deeper tissue linked with insulin resistance, higher triglycerides, lower HDL, and higher blood pressure over time. To keep screening simple, public health guidance uses waist cut points as a quick flag. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention cites more than 35 inches for women and more than 40 inches for men as thresholds associated with higher likelihood of cardiometabolic strain. Use those numbers as a prompt, not a label. If your waist sits above a cut point or trends upward over several months, look at the rest of your longevity baseline, especially blood pressure, lipids, and glucose, since those markers often shift together. If you want a height-adjusted option, use the waist-to-height ratio method. Measure your waist, divide it by your height, and keep units consistent for both numbers. In research , a 0.5 cutoff is often used as a simple screening threshold, meaning your waist stays under half your height. It’s not perfect, but it’s easy to calculate, it adjusts for body size, and it often tracks cardiometabolic risk more reliably than weight alone. One nuance matters here. Waist measurements shift for reasons beyond fat gain. Salt intake, travel, constipation, cycle-related fluid shifts, alcohol, stress, poor sleep, and inflammation can all move the number short term. One reading rarely tells you much. What matters is the pattern. When the waist measurement keeps rising across several months, that trend carries clinical signal. Where to keep track of waist size Keep waist size in your longevity baseline notes with three data points: Date Waist size Waist-to-height ratio, if you use it A monthly cadence works for most people. Weekly checks can create noise and frustration, especially when digestion, stress load, or hormones vary. What to do with a rising waist trend If your waist measurement starts trending upward, first look for the most likely drivers in your routine. Changes in sleep consistency, alcohol intake, meal timing, stress load, daily activity, and strength training often show up at the waist before they show up on a lab report. Waist trends also respond to the same fundamentals that improve lipids and blood sugar over time, especially consistent aerobic activity, resistance training, and fiber-forward eating patterns. If waist size keeps rising across several months, especially alongside higher blood pressure, rising triglycerides, lower HDL, or rising glucose, bring the trend into a clinical conversation. Waist size isn’t a diagnosis, but it can add clarity to the bigger metabolic picture and help guide next steps. Marker 10: Your Oral And Gum Health Your mouth is a living ecosystem with blood vessels, immune tissue, and a dense bacterial community. Healthy gums act like a tight seal around each tooth, keeping bacteria where they belong. When your gums get inflamed, they can loosen that seal. Tiny pockets can form along the gumline, giving bacteria more space to grow and more access to the bloodstream. Early inflammation may show up as bleeding when you brush or floss, mild tenderness, or persistent bad breath. Later, your gums may recede, teeth can feel sensitive, and pockets can deepen. By the time pain shows up, the process may already be advanced. Why oral and gum health matters for longevity Gum inflammation is a chronic inflammatory stressor with whole-body reach. Periodontal disease has been associated with higher cardiometabolic risk , because ongoing inflammation and bacterial exposure may influence vascular function. Gum disease also has a well-established relationship with diabetes . Poor glucose control can worsen gum inflammation, and untreated gum disease can make glucose control harder. From a healthspan perspective, gum health matters for two reasons. First, it’s a modifiable source of inflammation. Second, it’s a marker many people overlook until it becomes expensive, painful, or both. Protecting your gums is a direct way to protect chewing, nutrition, sleep quality, and long-term resilience. How to check your gum health in real life You don’t need special tools to spot early signals. You need a consistent quick scan. Pay attention to: Bleeding when brushing or flossing Swollen, puffy, or tender gums Bad breath that persists despite brushing Gum recession or teeth looking “longer” Tooth sensitivity near the gumline A tooth feeling loose or shifting One useful rule: healthy gums usually don’t bleed with gentle brushing or flossing. Occasional bleeding can happen if you’ve skipped flossing for a while, but bleeding that continues past a week or two is worth addressing. What “good” looks like A healthy baseline usually includes: Little to no bleeding with brushing or flossing Gums that look pink and firm, not swollen No persistent bad breath Dental cleanings and exams on a regular schedule During dental visits, your hygienist may measure gum pockets. Smaller pocket depths and low bleeding scores generally signal healthier gums. If your office tracks those numbers, they can become part of your baseline, especially if gum disease runs in your family, or you’ve had issues before. Where to keep track of oral health markers Keep oral health simple in your longevity baseline notes: Date of last dental exam and cleaning Any gum concerns noted by your dental team Periodontal measurements or “pocket depth” notes, if provided Treatment history, such as deep cleanings or gum therapy What to do if you notice gum changes If bleeding, tenderness, or swelling shows up, start with fundamentals and act early. Brush twice daily with a soft brush, clean between teeth daily with floss or interdental brushes, and stay consistent for two weeks. If bleeding persists or worsens, schedule a dental visit. Early gum inflammation is often far easier to reverse than established periodontal disease. If you live with diabetes , smoke or vape, or take medications that dry the mouth, gum care deserves extra attention. Those factors can raise risk for gum disease and accelerate progression. The goal stays the same: reduce inflammation early, protect the seal, and keep oral health from becoming a long-term stressor. Marker 11: Your Skin Map And Mole Checks Your skin is your largest organ, and it gives you something most organs do not: visibility. You can see change early, often before it causes pain or disrupts daily life. Skin checks belong in a longevity baseline for two reasons. First, the risk of skin cancer rises with cumulative sun exposure and age. Second, your “normal” skin pattern is personal. Once you know what belongs on your body, change becomes easier to spot. A skin map is simply a record of your usual landmarks. Moles, freckles, birthmarks, scars, and any spots you know well. The goal is familiarity. You’re building a baseline, so new or changing spots stand out. Why skin checks matter for longevity Skin cancers, including melanoma, are most treatable when caught early. Many serious lesions start as small visual changes. A regular self-check increases the odds you notice a change while treatment stays simpler. Skin checks also protect healthspan in a practical way. When you catch issues early, you reduce the chance of larger procedures, more scarring, or longer recovery. Early detection supports continuity in the life you want to keep living. How to do an skin self-check A good skin self-check is methodical and repeatable. Use a bright light, full-length mirror, and a hand mirror. Move head to toe in the same order each time, so you don’t skip areas. Pay attention to places people miss like your scalp, behind your ears, the back of your neck, under your breasts, between your fingers and toes, the soles of your feet, and the back side of your legs. You’re looking for two categories of change: a brand-new spot you haven’t seen before, or a spot you already know that looks different in size, shape, color, border, or sensation. Clinicians often teach the ABCDE lens for moles, since it provides a structured way to scan. Asymmetry, border irregularity, color variation, diameter growth, and evolving change in any direction. You don’t need every letter for a spot to deserve attention. “Evolving” carries a lot of clinical weight. Where to keep track of skin changes Keep skin tracking simple: A photo set on your phone in a dedicated album can work well, especially for areas hard to view. In your longevity baseline notes, record the date, location, and a short description for anything new or changing. Photos help because your memory can play tricks on you. A picture turns “I think this changed” into a clearer comparison across months. What to do if you find a concerning spot If you see a new spot that looks unusual, or a spot that’s clearly changing over weeks or months, schedule a dermatology visit. If you have high-risk factors, such as a personal or family history of melanoma, many atypical moles, blistering sunburn history, immune suppression, or significant outdoor exposure, routine professional skin exams may carry more value. Skin checks are not about obsessing. They are about pattern recognition. Baseline plus repeatability is what makes the marker useful. Marker 12: Your Blood Sugar And A1C Blood sugar is your bloodstream’s circulating fuel. Glucose moves through your blood so muscles, brain, and organs have energy available minute to minute. Insulin is the hormone that helps move glucose from blood into cells, where it can be used or stored. When insulin works well, blood sugar rises after eating, then returns toward baseline in a predictable curve. When insulin sensitivity declines, blood sugar stays higher for longer, and the system starts compensating by producing more insulin. A1C adds a longer lens. It reflects the average level of glucose exposure over the past few months, since glucose binds to hemoglobin in red blood cells. Think of it as a time-weighted summary, not a single-day snapshot. Why blood sugar matters for longevity Glucose regulation sits near the center of long-term cardiometabolic health. Over time, elevated glucose and insulin resistance increase risk for vascular disease, kidney disease, neuropathy, and vision changes. Even before diabetes enters the picture, subtle glucose drift can travel with rising triglycerides, lower HDL, higher blood pressure, and increasing waist size. Those markers tend to cluster because they share underlying physiology. From a healthspan perspective, blood sugar tracking matters because early stages often feel normal. When you catch changes early, options stay broader and usually stay simpler. How to get your blood sugar numbers and what they mean Most people start with three common tests: Fasting glucose, a single measurement after an overnight fast A1C, a multi-month average of glucose exposure Oral glucose tolerance testing, used when a clinician needs a deeper look at glucose handling after a glucose load Many labs include reference ranges, and clinicians interpret results in context of age, pregnancy status, medications, sleep patterns, stress load, and family history. In general U.S. criteria, fasting glucose under 100 mg/dL and A1C under 5.7 percent often fall in the normal range. Fasting glucose from 100 to 125 mg/dL or A1C from 5.7 to 6.4 percent often falls in a prediabetes range. Fasting glucose at or above 126 mg/dL or A1C at or above 6.5 percent can meet criteria for diabetes when confirmed in the appropriate clinical context. The clinical goal is not a single perfect number. The goal is stability over time, plus early action when blood glucose readings increase. Where to keep track of blood sugar markers In your longevity baseline notes, keep the dates and headline results for A1C and fasting glucose so you can see trends quickly without digging through records. Any additional context your clinician highlights, such as “repeat in six months” or “focus on post-meal spikes.” This practice give you fast access to trends without digging through portals. What to do with a rising trend If A1C or fasting glucose starts rising across repeat testing, focus on the fundamentals that most consistently improve glucose handling: sleep consistency, strength training, aerobic activity, meal composition with adequate fiber and protein, and alcohol frequency. Those inputs influence insulin sensitivity in measurable ways. If your routine has been stable and numbers still rise, or if you have a strong family history of diabetes, bring the trend into a clinician conversation so you can tailor screening cadence and next steps. Blood sugar is one of the clearest examples of longevity medicine in real life. Early upward changes rarely cause symptoms today, but they can shape how your next decade feels. How To Use Your Longevity Baseline Longevity becomes practical when your baseline is easy to maintain and easy to reference. You’ve now got a core set of markers that cover three jobs: a few high-impact facts you keep on file, daily-life signals that reflect how your body is functioning week to week, and medical benchmarks that reveal risk long before symptoms force action. Keep the system simple. Let a wearable or phone app capture passive data like sleep, steps, and resting heart rate. Keep a single baseline note with dates and headline numbers for labs, screenings, blood pressure averages, and any updates to personal or family history. When you check in, focus on trend direction. One unusual reading rarely means much. A consistent change across weeks or months earns attention. When one marker starts moving in the wrong direction, don’t treat it like a personal failure or a mystery. Treat it like feedback. Most longevity markers respond to a short list of inputs: sleep consistency, aerobic activity, strength training, alcohol intake, nutrition patterns (especially fiber and protein), stress load, and follow-through on recommended care. Pick the one input that most realistically fits your life right now, tighten it for a set window of time, then recheck the marker on an appropriate cadence so you can see whether the trend changes. Small adjustments, repeated, may shift markers in meaningful ways over time. Your baseline makes those adjustments smarter, because you’re responding to real signals instead of guesswork. Most importantly, use your baseline to improve clinical conversations. A simple record of your typical ranges, key dates, and recent trends helps your care team assess risk faster and tailor screening or next steps with more precision. Longevity isn’t a single habit. It’s a long game of consistency, early awareness, and course correction you can keep doing in real life.
